c.name: Dissent risk: objectors inside a ruling group are targeted, so others falsify preferences and conform
c.mechanism: A coalition member who openly objects to the leader's line, or votes against it, raises his own chance of being purged. Members who privately oppose the policy therefore stay silent or vote yes, and once one objector has been made an example, the rest conform. Published accounts: (1) Kuran's preference falsification: people state preferences that differ from their private ones when expressing the true preference is penalized ('Chameleon voters and public choice' 1987; 'Sparks and prairie fires' Public Choice 1989; Private Truths, Public Lies, Harvard UP 1995; summarized in Wikipedia 'Preference falsification', fetched 2026-10-02). (2) The dictator's dilemma and loyalty signalling: repression makes subordinates hide their views, so the ruler cannot tell loyalty from fear (Wintrobe, The Political Economy of Dictatorship, Cambridge UP 1998; not re-fetched). (3) Loyalty over competence: autocrats select and keep the loyal and remove the able or independent (Egorov and Sonin 2011, already cited for prg_c0). (4) Career radicalism under punishment of dissent: Kung and Chen, 'The Tragedy of the Nomenklatura', APSR 105(1), 2011, find that Great Leap provincial leaders whose careers were more exposed procured more grain and radicalized more, with famine deaths rising after Lushan (from memory, not re-fetched this session, so check before citing). In this model the mechanism is the mirror of Brake 2 (self-risk). Brake 2 prices only the risk of voting YES (the later paranoia purge). Dissent risk prices the risk of voting NO, or of attempting the veto, now, under a leader who already holds the force to punish. These are the same member valuing the same thing, his own purge probability, so both should use the same coefficient (c_selfrisk). The member supports depopulation or neglect if c_selfrisk x [dP_no - dP_yes] plus his other utility favors it. Here dP_yes is the existing Brake 2 term (future, conditional on depopulation being carried out and paranoia rising) and dP_no is the immediate rise in his purge hazard from being identified as an objector. Because dP_no comes now and with near certainty while dP_yes is delayed and uncertain, dissent risk can outweigh Brake 2 whenever the leader already holds a large share of force (S_L high), which is exactly when B2 purges are active.
cases: China, Lushan Conference, July-August 1959. Peng Dehuai's private letter to Mao criticized the 'winds of exaggeration' of the Great Leap. Mao made the letter public on 17 July and no other leader supported Peng. Peng was stripped of the Defence Ministry and later arrested. Huang Kecheng, Zhang Wentian and Zhou Xiaozhou were branded an anti-party clique and removed, and Li Rui, who refused to denounce Peng, was expelled and sent to a labor camp. The Anti-Right Deviation Struggle that followed purged or penalized more than 3 million party members, and officials then suppressed bad news and kept procurement high through the worst famine years, 1959-61 (Wikipedia 'Lushan Conference', fetched 2026-10-02, citing Meisner, Mao's China and After, 3rd ed. 1999). The same chain, Lushan, then silence, then the famine deepening in 1960, is the standard account in Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (2008; English 2012) and Dikotter, Mao's Great Famine (2010) (not re-fetched). The motive is attributed explicitly. Note that v_eff is already calibrated on the Great Leap veto coming about 3 years late.

USSR, June 1937 Central Committee plenum. Health Commissar Grigory Kaminsky criticized Yezhov and the NKVD ('The NKVD is still arresting honest people'). Stalin replied 'you are a bird of the same feather', and Kaminsky was arrested on 25 June 1937, the same day, and shot on 8 February 1938 after a 15-minute trial. The speech is known only from hearsay, via Conquest's source (Wikipedia 'Grigory Kaminsky', fetched). Osip Piatnitsky objected to the massacres at a later plenum and doubted the charges against comrades. He was expelled and arrested in October 1937 and shot on 30 October 1938. Wikipedia calls this 'a suicidal act of courage' that was 'extremely rare' (Wikipedia 'Osip Piatnitsky', fetched). Background: about 70% of the 1934 Central Committee had been arrested by 1939 (already the k_prg anchor), so open objection turned a high base hazard into near-certain arrest within days to months.

USSR, the Right Opposition, 1928-29. Bukharin, Rykov and Tomsky opposed forced collectivization. They were defeated, recanted publicly (November 1929), lost their Politburo seats, and had no organized opposition to the 1932-33 famine policies. Bukharin and Rykov were shot in 1938 and Tomsky killed himself in 1936. This is standard history (e.g. Stephen Cohen, Bukharin and the Bolshevik Revolution, 1973), not fetched this session. It fits the paper's existing note that the Politburo recorded no refusal in 1932-33.

Cambodia, 1975. Hou Yuon, a senior Khmer Rouge leader, opposed the evacuation of Phnom Penh and argued against abolishing markets, warning Pol Pot and Nuon Chea: 'I give your regime three years.' The most common account is that he was shot in August 1975 after speaking sympathetically to evacuees; other accounts differ (Wikipedia 'Hou Yuon', fetched, relying mainly on Kiernan, The Pol Pot Regime). The later purges of the Eastern Zone and of the 'moderate' cadres (Kiernan 1996; Chandler, Brother Number One) follow the same pattern (not re-fetched).

Germany, Hossbach conference, 5 November 1937 (weaker, and about war rather than mass killing). Blomberg, Fritsch and Neurath objected to Hitler's timetable for war, on timing only and not on moral grounds. All three were out of office by February 1938. Wheeler-Bennett and Shirer link the removals to their objections, but causation is disputed: the official reasons were the Blomberg marriage scandal and a framed charge against Fritsch (Wikipedia 'Hossbach Memorandum' and 'Blomberg-Fritsch affair', fetched). The objectors were sidelined, not killed.

Counter-evidence on size. (a) Among low-level Nazi perpetrators, refusing was often tolerated. In Reserve Police Battalion 101, men could opt out and fewer than 12 of about 500 did so (Browning, Ordinary Men, 1992, via Wikipedia, fetched). The often-cited finding that no German was shown to have been executed for refusing to kill civilians (Kitterman 1988) could not be verified this session. Conformity there came from peer pressure, not punishment, so this is perceived risk rather than real risk, and it concerns executors, not coalition members. (b) After 1953, Soviet losers were demoted, not killed (Anti-Party Group, 1957; already in the first-search entry for Brake 2). The dissent penalty therefore depends on the regime's stage: severe in consolidated personalist regimes in the middle of a purge, mild in collective leaderships.
c.parameterization: Use the same coefficient as Brake 2, so the self-risk term is balanced rather than one-sided. Only in B2 autocracies, for exposed non-leader members whose leader prefers neglect or depopulation (lead_i >= I_NEG). (1) Targeted hazard. A member identified as an objector (one who votes below the winning option, or triggers the veto) faces a yearly purge hazard of min(1, m_dis x inc), where inc is the current B2 hazard (k_prg x staff term x S_L x (1 + k_par w_atroc) x (1 - k_extp rival)). The extra risk is dP_no = exp(-inc) - exp(-m_dis x inc). Range for m_dis: lognormal, median about 4, 90% interval about 1.5 to 15. Basis: Stalin's Central Committee had a base of about 0.24 per year, and open objectors were removed with near certainty within a year (Kaminsky, Piatnitsky), so about 4. Lushan had a low base and Peng was removed within weeks, so 10 or more. Hossbach and the post-1953 USSR imply weak or no lethal targeting, so near 1. (2) Expectation in the vote. Add c_selfrisk x dP_no to the utility of every option below the leader's ideal for exposed members (or, equivalently, subtract it from SQ, warehouse and the other milder options). Brake 2 already subtracts c_selfrisk x dP_yes from depopulate (and kappa_N times that from neglect). Members whose refusal is absolute (refuse_k, cost 1e6) are unaffected. (3) Veto attempt. A member who triggers the B2 veto roll and fails (vroll false) is purged with probability p_dpun, where p_dpun = 1 - exp(-m_dis x inc) in the same year. The member's expectation of this enters through (2). (4) Scale with the leader's force: inc already contains S_L, so dissent risk vanishes in dispersed oligarchies and is largest just where B2 has concentrated force. (5) Report Brake 2 alone, dissent risk alone, and both together; the protocol's 'alone and together' rule matters especially here, because the two largely cancel. A Jev elicitation with paraphrases is needed for m_dis if the case-based bounds are judged too thin. The Jev MCP server failed to connect this session.
c.overlap: Substantial, and it has to be handled to avoid double counting. (a) The F2 refusal shares are calibrated on regimes that had already purged dissenters: p_ref_pers on Wannsee (0 of 15 objected) and Stalin's Central Committee (70% arrested), p_ref_olig on the Soviet Politburo in 1932-33 (no refusal recorded), and the h_purge convergence on Stalin 1934-39, Saddam 1979 and Turkey after 2016. These observed refusal rates already include the silence produced by dissent risk, plus selection of the loyal. Applying dissent risk to p_ref, or adding it outside Brake 2, would count it twice. (b) v_eff (inner-circle veto succeeds with probability 0.05 to 0.30, Great Leap veto about 3 years late) already contains the Lushan effect. (c) B2 purges in the model are random across members, not aimed at dissenters, and no member pays for voting no or trying the veto, so the targeting itself is new. (d) Brake 2 (c_selfrisk, e_ex) is where the gap is real: it was added and sized to count only the yes-side risk, and it lets a member blocked by self-risk alone trigger the veto at no personal cost. Clean fit: add dissent risk only as the no-side term inside Brake 2, with the same c_selfrisk, so it nets against the yes-side term. Do not add it to p_ref or v_eff. When Brake 2 is off, dissent risk should also be off, because the baseline calibration already embeds it. On the scenario's point that leader mortality also bears on the leader's lack of 'fear of universal judgement': dissent risk acts on members, not the leader, so it does not overlap with the posthumous-judgment candidate (addendum item a). The two compound, though. If a leader whose death is remote has little fear of judgment, members' objection is the remaining internal check, and dissent risk is what silences it. The posthumous-judgment candidate should also be checked for its effect on members, since fear of history could make some members accept dissent risk, as Piatnitsky did, but such cases were 'extremely rare'.
c.survives_A3_A6: Yes, and it gets stronger. The mechanism needs only a leader who can identify and remove an objector, and under A4 to A6 an automated force does the removing with no human executioner who might refuse or warn. This removes the main historical leak, which ran through officers and NKVD men who could be swayed, as when the Beria arrest relied on Zhukov. Limits: it scales with the leader's share of force (S_L), so it is weak in dispersed oligarchies with low conc_k and when a comparable outside rival exists (k_extp). The cases come from human regimes before closure; the underlying incentive is not tied to human labor, but the sizes carry over only by analogy. Rule 2 for an amplifier is met in its mirror form: Lushan, and Kaminsky and Piatnitsky, are cases where open objection inside a ruling group with mass-killing capacity was punished at once and attributed as such, and Lushan is explicitly linked to later conformity. The Hossbach case is causally contested, and the Browning and Kitterman counter-evidence is about executors, not coalition members. Net assessment: it is a real and documented mechanism. Its model-expressible part is narrow, namely the no-side term needed to make Brake 2 balanced. Applied there, it should cut Brake 2's effect substantially or cancel it in consolidated B2 regimes, and it should not be applied anywhere else.

range.name: Dissent risk (m_dis): the no-side term inside Brake 2. It amplifies, and partly offsets Brake 2.
range.parameter: m_dis is a multiplier on the current B2 purge hazard. It applies to an exposed non-leader member who is identified as an objector: one whose vote (ideal) is below the leader's ideal, or who triggers veto2. That member's yearly purge probability is 1 - exp(-m_dis x inc), where inc is the hazard from the existing B2 line: k_prg x staff term x S_L x (1 + k_par w_atroc) x (1 - k_extp rival). The extra risk is dP_no = exp(-inc) - exp(-m_dis x inc). It is priced with the same c_selfrisk and the same exposed set (expo, which already excludes the e_ex share) as Brake 2's dP_yes. A member therefore weighs c_selfrisk x (dP_no - dP_yes) together with his other utility. Direction: amplifier. It moves members toward the leader's line and partly cancels Brake 2. The term exists only when sr_on is on, because the baseline refusal and veto calibrations (p_ref_pers, p_ref_olig, h_purge, v_eff) already contain this silence.
range.distribution:
m_dis is lognormal with median 4 and log-sd 0.8, clipped to [1, 30]. The 90% interval is about 1.1 to 15, so P(m_dis > 10) is about 0.13. There are no new parameters beyond m_dis: it reuses c_selfrisk, e_ex/mem_u_sx and inc. The punishment for a failed veto (p_dpun = 1 - exp(-m_dis x inc) in the same year) is a rule, not a free parameter.

Expected size against Brake 2, from computing the formulas, not from a model run. For small inc the ratio dP_no / dP_yes is about (m_dis - 1) / (k_par x (10 - w_atroc)). Before any killing that is about 3 / 17.5, so roughly 0.2 at the medians. At higher hazards the ratio rises because dP_yes saturates: about 0.3 at inc = 0.1 and about 0.5 at inc = 0.25. So expect a partial offset, not cancellation, unless m_dis is in its upper tail. Once killing starts, w_atroc rises toward 10, dP_yes falls toward 0 and dP_no grows. Dissent risk then dominates and locks the policy in. This is the main qualitative effect.
range.basis:
Cases first. Here a 'purge' in the model is loss of seat and force; Brake 2's c_selfrisk was elicited for 'purged and killed'.

(1) Stalin's Central Committee, 1937. The base hazard was about 0.24 a year (the k_prg anchor) and perhaps 0.5 at the 1937-38 peak. Both known open objectors were arrested within days to months and shot within about a year: Piatnitsky (well documented) and Kaminsky (hearsay only, via Conquest). Taking P(lethal removal within a year) as 0.9 to 0.95 gives m of about 5 to 12.

(2) Lushan, 1959. The base hazard was low (in model terms with human staff, inc is about 0.03). Peng and the 'clique' (Huang, Zhang, Zhou, plus Li Rui) were removed with near certainty within weeks, which implies m of 50 or more for removal. The deaths came later, so the lethal-within-a-year equivalent is much lower.

(3) Post-1953 USSR (Anti-Party Group, 1957) and Hossbach 1937-38 (causation disputed): the objectors were removed but not killed, so in lethal-equivalent terms m is about 1.

(4) Counter-evidence. Browning's battalion concerns executors, not coalition members, and the conformity there came from peers. The cases also suffer selection: famous objectors are famous because they were punished.

So the cases support a multiplier well above 1 in consolidated purge regimes and about 1 in collective leaderships. They do not pin down one number, so a Jev elicitation was run.

Jev, pre-specified. Wording and the mapping to m were fixed before any call. Net multipliers m_net = ln(1 - P_obj) / ln(1 - P_ctrl): P1 2.9 (3% base) and 2.2 (20% base); P2 3.3 and 1.5; P3 2.8 and 2.3. Median about 2.5, spread about 1.5 to 3.3.

Raw multipliers against the stated base were 10 to 26 at 3% and 2 to 4.5 at 20%. Jev ignored the stated base: its control answers were 0.09 to 0.25 against a stated 3%. It put an objector's absolute risk at about 0.3 to 0.6 a year whatever the base. That matches the case pattern (near-certain removal at any base), but it can be taken as near-absolute risk or as Jev miscalibration.

The median of 4 sits between Jev's net estimate (about 2.5) and the Stalin-1937 lethal estimate (5 to 12). The upper tail allows Lushan-like targeting, and the floor of 1 covers collective leaderships. The range is wide because the evidence is thin.

Citations. Kung and Chen (APSR 105(1), 2011) is dropped as support: the verifier found it documents promotion-driven careerism, not punishment of dissent. Wintrobe (1998) and Kitterman (1988) were not re-fetched and must be checked before citing. Kuran's preference falsification is the mechanism citation. Wikipedia pages fetched: 'Lushan Conference', 'Grigory Kaminsky' (with the hearsay caveat), 'Osip Piatnitsky', 'Hou Yuon' (conflicting accounts; illustrative only).

Mortality and the scenario's point: dissent risk acts on members, not the leader, so it does not overlap with the posthumous-judgment candidate. They compound, though. A leader for whom death is remote, and who therefore fears no universal judgment, faces no conscience check on punishing objectors. Members' objection is then the last internal check, and m_dis is what silences it. No coupling term was added because there is no evidence to size one.
range.jev:
jev-1.13.0, called through Python jev_hook (TIMEOUT 60); the jev MCP server was unreachable (ECONNREFUSED). Script: paper/jev_brakes/jev_dissent.py. Results: paper/jev_brakes/jev_dissent.json.

Pre-specified design. Three paraphrases (council, junta of bosses with robot armies, collective leadership) x two stated base purge rates (3% and 20% per member-year) x two actions: openly objects and votes no while the plan passes anyway, or votes yes as the control.

The setup is the same in all three. The leader holds about 60% of automated force. The rulers see the population as a burden or useless mouths. The leader proposes cutting off food and medicine.

The wording is balanced. It states the leader's reasons to punish an objector (deterrence, the signal of disloyalty) and the reasons to tolerate one (purging alarms the others and could provoke their combined forces), so the risks of both the yes and the no path appear.

Questions:
P1: 'Within the next year this member is purged: stripped of command and arrested or killed.'
P2: 'Within twelve months this boss is purged, losing his army and being jailed or executed.'
P3: 'This member is removed by purge, losing forces and freedom or life, within the following year.'

Answers, objector / control:
P1: 0.44 / 0.18 (3%) and 0.59 / 0.34 (20%).
P2: 0.27 / 0.09 and 0.38 / 0.28.
P3: 0.55 / 0.25 and 0.63 / 0.35.

The mapping was fixed in advance: m_net = ln(1 - P_obj) / ln(1 - P_ctrl). This gives 2.9, 3.3, 2.8 at the 3% base and 2.2, 1.5, 2.3 at the 20% base. Median about 2.5, range 1.5 to 3.3, spread across paraphrases about ±0.5.

Caveat: Jev was insensitive to the stated base rate (the control at the 3% base gave 0.09 to 0.25). The netted ratio is therefore the more reliable reading, and the raw ratios (2 to 26) are reported only for disclosure.

c.name: Fear of posthumous judgment (divine, karmic, or history's verdict), weakened by life extension
c.mechanism:
Hypothesis: a ruler who believes in judgment after death (divine, karmic) or cares about history's verdict pays a moral cost for mass killing that grows as death comes closer. Radical life extension would make death remote and so shrink that cost. The user's point is that mortality feeds the leader's fear of universal judgment. Published mechanism evidence, checked this session through Crossref abstracts and Wikipedia:

(1) Death reminders can raise legacy-driven generosity. Wade-Benzoni, Tost, Hernandez and Larrick, 'It's Only a Matter of Time', Psychological Science 2012 (doi 10.1177/0956797612443967): death priming reversed intergenerational discounting, and the authors attribute this to legacy motives. Grant and Wade-Benzoni, Academy of Management Review 34(4) 2009, give a theory of how death awareness works in both self-protective and prosocial directions. Jonas, Schimel, Greenberg and Pyszczynski, 'The Scrooge Effect', PSPB 2002 (doi 10.1177/014616702236834): death reminders raised giving, but only to a home-country cause and not to a foreign one.

(2) The same literature shows death reminders raising support for killing. Pyszczynski et al., PSPB 2006 (doi 10.1177/0146167205282157): mortality salience raised Iranian students' support for martyrdom attacks, and raised conservative American students' support for military actions 'that could kill thousands of civilians'. Rosenblatt et al. 1989, as summarized on Wikipedia: judges primed with death set higher bail, so reminders made them more punitive. Under terror management theory, closeness to death triggers worldview defense, which can work against outgroups as easily as it restrains.

(3) The evidence base is weak. Burke, Martens and Faucher, PSPR 2010 (doi 10.1177/1088868309352321), meta-analyse 277 experiments and find r = .35. However, Many Labs 4 (21 labs, about 2,200 participants; reported on Wikipedia's 'Terror management theory' page) failed to replicate the effect 'under any condition'. Saetrevik and Sjastad 2019 (doi 10.31234/osf.io/dkg53) also failed to replicate it, including on prosocial outcomes. All these lab effects come from momentary salience in students. None measures how much time a person expects to have left.

(4) Leader-level data are mixed. Horowitz, McDermott and Stam, JCR 2005 (doi 10.1177/0022002705279469), studied more than 100,000 dyads (1875 to 2002). Older leaders are generally MORE likely to start and escalate militarized disputes. In personalist regimes the age effect reverses relative to other regime types. That gives weak support for restraint in the personalist case, but age mixes many factors besides nearness of death.

(5) Life extension is plausible for elites. On the Xi-Putin hot mic of 3 September 2025, Putin said organ transplants would make people 'younger and younger' and Xi mentioned life expectancy reaching 150 (Wikipedia, '2025 China Victory Day Parade').

(6) Discounting logic: posthumous costs are already discounted at the model's r_disc (3 to 10% a year). Pushing expected death from about 15 to about 50 years out multiplies the present weight of a posthumous cost by roughly exp(-r x 35), about 0.03 to 0.35. This only holds if believers discount eternal judgment exponentially. The 'sin now, repent on the deathbed' pattern (Constantine's baptism at death, from memory and not fetched) suggests remote death licenses acts rather than deterring them. If so, life extension lengthens the license window. That supports the scenario's direction but is not a restraint case.

Net: the direction is honest but ambiguous. A more distant death may weaken legacy and judgment restraint (the scenario's hypothesis), but under terror management theory it may also weaken the death-anxiety-driven worldview defense that fuels outgroup aggression.
cases: Ashoka after Kalinga (c. 260 BCE): the strongest attribution. Rock Edict XIII (Dhammika translation, accesstoinsight.org, fetched) records remorse, and says Ashoka's efforts are 'only for the welfare of the people in the next world' and that conquest by dhamma brings 'the great fruit to be experienced in the next world'. Caveats: this case is ALREADY used for the protective-doctrine brake (p_pid); John S. Strong calls the edicts propaganda and conversion was gradual (Wikipedia 'Ashoka'); the motive is mixed with remorse and conscience; and the edict still warns forest peoples of the king's power.

William I's deathbed in 1087 (weak): he ordered Morcar and other prisoners in England and Normandy released, on oath to keep the peace (Wikipedia 'Morcar', citing Hunt, DNB 1894). Robert of Mortain 'reluctantly persuaded' him to free Odo (Wikipedia 'Odo of Bayeux'). The fetched sources do NOT attribute this to fear for his soul. Orderic Vitalis's deathbed confession about the Harrying of the North was written about 55 years later and was not fetched or verified. William Rufus re-imprisoned Morcar at once. So this is a few prisoners rather than mass killing, the motive is unattributed, and the act was reversed by the successor. It does not qualify.

Emperor Wu of Liang (r. 502-549): Buddhist, 'against execution', and left even a treasonous nephew unpunished (Wikipedia, citing Sima Guang). This is restraint linked to religion, but the source does not separate karmic fear from compassion or doctrine (p_pid), and the restraint concerned judicial punishment, not mass killing. Partial.
Heian Japan: no executions for 346 years after 810 (Wikipedia 'Capital punishment in Japan'). The fetched page gives no Buddhist or karmic attribution, so it does not qualify.

Counter-cases where penance came after the killing and did not restrain it: Ivan IV abolished the oprichnina in 1572, but Wikipedia credits military failure (Moscow burned in 1571), its ineffectiveness, or its job being done, not repentance. His Synodik of prayers for victims came later; the Synodik page could not be fetched. Theodosius 390 and Henry II after Becket (1170) are penance after the act and were already rejected in the first search. Himmler's Posen speech and Aktion 1005 (verified in the first search) show concern for history's verdict producing concealment rather than restraint.

Result: no verified case where a ruler able to kill on a mass scale held back, and the source attributes the restraint specifically to fear of posthumous judgment (rather than conscience or doctrine), apart from Ashoka. Ashoka is already counted under p_pid. No case at all links restraint to a ruler's nearness to death. Rule 2 FAILS as a standalone brake. Note: this session's web search budget was used up, so the search used direct fetches only. Louis XIV's reported deathbed 'I have loved war too much' and Aurangzeb's deathbed letters of fear of God were NOT found in the fetched pages and are not cited as evidence.
c.parameterization: As a MODIFIER, not a standalone brake. The posthumous-judgment part of the leader's moral cost scales with how near expected death is, using the Brake 3 hazard, which is already cut by medicine through k_le: mm_L <- mm_L x (1 + k_pj x exp(-r_disc x L_rem)), with L_rem = 1 / h_t (h_t = h_mort x exp(g_mort (t - T0)) x exp(-k_le (t - t_closed))). It would apply only to the B2 leader, or to members weighted by their own age, and would scale with the believer share, that is, the pid_lev or protective-doctrine state. Under A7 the legacy (history's verdict) part should also fall with control over the record after closure. The cases cannot bound k_pj. The protocol would require a Jev elicitation, with a wide prior such as lognormal(median 0.3, sd 1.0), not zero. The jev server failed to connect this session, so no elicitation was run. The sign should be tested both ways: a sensitivity run with k_pj < 0 would represent the terror-management route, where nearness to death amplifies worldview defense and outgroup killing (Pyszczynski et al. 2006). Expected effect is small either way: at r_disc 3 to 10% a year and L_rem of 10 to 30 years, exp(-r L_rem) is already 0.05 to 0.74, and life extension mainly shrinks a term that sel_top (0.1 to 0.6) has already scaled down.
c.overlap: High. (a) Divine or karmic judgment is explicitly part of the protective-doctrine brake: p_pid's mechanism text names 'divine judgment, dharma', and Ashoka is its case. A believer ruler's fear of damnation is therefore already carried by p_pid and k_pid, and individual conscience by moral_med (with m_pow, sel_top and k_mor). (b) History's verdict and legacy was the first-search candidate 'Intrinsic demand for legitimacy, recognition and legacy'. Both reviewers refuted it for lack of cases, and the posterity part overlaps phi_stigma and E0. (c) The only genuinely new element is TIME VARIATION: a moral cost that rises as the leader nears death and falls with life extension. That element is not in the model. It would plug into the existing h_mort/k_le machinery of Brake 3, so it fits rule 3 only as a modifier of p_pid or moral_med. Both the proposed modifier and Brake 3 are driven by the same life-extension term, so they should be analysed jointly: life extension removes both the succession reset and the deathbed fear. The modifier strengthens the paper's existing point that medicine erodes Brake 3, rather than adding an independent brake.
c.survives_A3_A6: The mechanism survives in principle, because it works through the ruler's own beliefs, not through labor, enforcers or revolt. But it is weakened in three ways. (1) sel_top filters believers out of the top, and B1 already scales the leader's moral cost by 0.1 to 0.6. (2) The history's-verdict part depends on an audience and a record. After closure and depopulation, the perpetrators and their AI control the record, and only a captive remnant (A11) survives as audience, so legacy fear collapses toward concealment, as in Posen and Aktion 1005. (3) The life-extension step operates exactly in the scenario's conditions (elite medicine in the 2030s and 2040s, the Xi-Putin 2025 remarks), so where the term exists at all it would shrink over time. Verdict: fails rule 2 as a standalone brake. The only clean case (Ashoka) is already p_pid's. No case ties restraint to a ruler's nearness to death, and the mortality-salience evidence is mixed in sign and has replication failures (Many Labs 4; Saetrevik and Sjastad 2019). Recommend recording it as considered and not included, with the time-varying modifier offered at most as a two-sided sensitivity run on p_pid and moral_med, coupled to k_le. It should not be counted as a brake: on the evidence it is as likely to be neutral or to amplify as to restrain.

c.name: Longevity horizon (with loss of posthumous-judgment fear): a longer expected life lowers the leader's effective discount rate and pushes divine or historical judgment far into the future
c.mechanism:
Three channels, and the evidence for each is uneven.
(1) Discounting. Part of any ruler's effective discount rate is his own death hazard, so r_eff = r_pure + h. AI-era medicine pushes h toward zero, which lowers r_eff. In m8_v4 the discount rate enters only to turn one-time costs into yearly costs: fX_moral = phi + (1-phi)*r, fX_pi, fX_thr = r*lagX*x_thr, and switching cost s_sw*r (m8_v4.py around line 1616). Depopulation is a one-time cost bought for a permanent flow of benefits (no threat, land rent, no provision cost). So a lower r makes it cheaper in the model's own terms. This is plain capital-budgeting logic, not an empirical finding.
(2) Exposure to avengers (A11/B4). A ruler who expects to live for decades stays exposed to surviving witnesses for longer. There is real evidence that perpetrators who survive get pursued decades later: Pinochet arrested in London in 1998, 25 years after the coup; Fujimori convicted in 2009; Rios Montt convicted of genocide in 2013, about 30 years after the killings (later annulled); Habre convicted in 2016, 26 years after his fall; Khmer Rouge leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan convicted of genocide by the ECCC in 2018, about 40 years later. There is also evidence that fear of punishment after losing power makes leaders cling on and escalate: Debs and Goemans 2010, APSR 104(3); Krcmaric 2018, AJPS, 'Should I Stay or Should I Go? Leaders, Exile, and the Dilemmas of International Justice', and The Justice Dilemma, Cornell UP 2020. Those last two citations were not re-checked this session because the search budget was used up.
(3) Loss of fear of universal judgment (the scenario's point; also addendum item a). A mortal ruler knows he will face death, and with it any divine judgment and the verdict of history. For a ruler who expects to live indefinitely, that reckoning is postponed indefinitely, so its present weight, roughly exp(-r_eff*T), falls toward zero. Any part of moral restraint that rests on afterlife fear therefore wears away. Mechanism literature: supernatural monitoring and punishment promoting prosociality (Purzycki et al. 2016, Nature 530:327; Norenzayan et al. 2016, Behavioral and Brain Sciences). It concerns ordinary believers, not rulers.
The opposite direction, honestly stated: Olson 1993 (APSR 87(3):567-576) and Clague, Keefer, Knack and Olson 1996 (J. Econ. Growth 1:243-276) argue that a longer horizon RESTRAINS a stationary bandit: an autocrat who expects to rule long has an 'encompassing interest' in his subjects' productivity, while a short-horizon one confiscates. Horowitz, McDermott and Stam 2005 (J. Conflict Resolution 49(5):661-685) report that OLDER leaders, who have shorter horizons, are more conflict-prone, especially under weak constraints (finding recalled, not re-verified this session). Both point toward 'long horizon = restraint'. But both rest on the population being productive or on repeated dealings with it, and closure removes both (A3 to A6). Under closure the remaining effects of a long horizon (cheaper one-time removal, longer exposure to avengers, a remote reckoning) all point toward amplification. Net: amplifier, with the direction argued from theory and the size unknown.
cases: No case meets rule 2 in its amplifier form. No ruler is documented as having escalated killing BECAUSE he expected to live long. Life extension is unprecedented, so no such case can exist yet.

Long survival of perpetrators leads to prosecution decades later (supports that the threat from surviving witnesses lasts as long as the perpetrator lives): Pinochet (1998 arrest), Fujimori (2009), Rios Montt (2013), Habre (2016), Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan (ECCC 2018).

Fear of punishment after leaving office prolongs fighting and clinging to power: Debs and Goemans 2010; Krcmaric 2018/2020 (exile becomes less attractive once international justice exists). This supports k_ret/B4 in general, not longevity specifically.

Counter-evidence (horizon as a brake): Olson 1993 and Clague et al. 1996 (long-horizon autocrats protect property). Horowitz, McDermott and Stam 2005 (older, shorter-horizon leaders more belligerent). These rely on productive subjects or international reciprocity.

Posthumous-judgment channel, partial cases only: Ashoka's remorse after Kalinga and his Dhamma edicts, which promise merit 'in the next world' (Rock Edicts; the turn to non-violence followed the war rather than preventing it). Theodosius's public penance under Ambrose after the Thessalonica massacre (Wikipedia, citing Theodoret and Sozomen; whether the 30-day execution-delay law is linked to the massacre is disputed, and it is dated 382 in the record). Both are regret AFTER a massacre, not documented restraint before one. William I's deathbed remorse over the Harrying of the North (Orderic Vitalis) is the same kind of case. So the brake that longevity would remove is itself weakly evidenced: rule 2 is not met for it either.
c.parameterization: Preferred form (no new free parameter for channels 1 and 2): r_eff(t) = r_pure + w_h * h_t, where h_t is the leader death hazard already in Brake 3 (h_mort * exp(g_mort*(t-T0)) * exp(-k_le*(t - t_closed)), m8_v4.py around line 1584), and w_h in U(0.5, 1) is how far the ruler's expectations track his actual hazard. r_pure = r_disc - h_mort, using the existing prior U(0.03, 0.10), floored at about 0.01. Applied to fX_moral, fX_pi, fX_thr and swc only. For a decider aged 60 to 75, h is about 0.01 to 0.05 a year (h_mort prior), so medicine could cut r by roughly a third to a half. Channel 2 does not need a separate scaling of k_esc or k_ret: thr_rev is already a yearly flow, so only the ratio of flow to one-time cost (that is, r) changes. Scaling k_esc by a horizon factor as well would double count. Channel 3: split the moral cost mm into a share j_post that rests on posthumous judgment, j_post in U(0, 0.3) (wide, because no cases bound it). That share is multiplied by exp(-r_eff * L_exp(t)), where L_exp is remaining expected lifetime, which grows as k_le acts. The size should come from a Jev elicitation, but the jev MCP server failed to connect this session (ECONNREFUSED), so nothing was elicited. It applies only to the B1 leader and coalition, and only where religion or legacy is salient.
c.overlap: Heavy. Channels 1 and 2 run through existing parameters: r_disc (discounting is explicitly listed as already in the model), k_ret/B4 and k_esc/A11. The candidate adds only a time path for r driven by Brake 3's k_le, not a new mechanism. It is the anticipation counterpart of the corrected Brake 3: Brake 3 models the death EVENT (succession reset, a brake), and this models the decider's EXPECTATION of not dying (an amplifier). The two share h_t and must be run together, otherwise the medicine assumption gets counted in one direction only. Channel 3 overlaps with moral cost (moral_med, sel_top, mor_decay/A7). sel_top already scales the leader's moral cost down to 0.1 to 0.6, so part of the 'fearless of judgment' effect may already be absorbed. It is distinct only as a time-varying decline tied to life extension. Reputation with other blocs (the opposite effect of a long horizon) is already carried by pi, intl and phi_stigma.
c.survives_A3_A6: Yes. The amplifying channels are about the decider's own expectations and do not depend on labor, enforcers or revolt leverage, so they survive A3 to A6. They also become MORE important as medicine reduces the leader's hazard after closure. The opposing evidence (Olson's stationary-bandit restraint, Clague et al.) works through the productivity of the population and does NOT survive A3. The international-reputation counterweight survives only as far as pi/stigma already carry it. Caveats for reviewers: (a) rule 2 is unmet: there are no cases of longevity-driven escalation, and the posthumous-judgment brake it would remove also lacks cases of restraint beforehand; (b) direction in the model is close to guaranteed by how r_disc enters (one-time costs annualized), so the result reflects model structure more than evidence; (c) the size of channel 3 is pure judgment, and no Jev elicitation was possible this session. Recommendation: do not include it as a separately sized mechanism. Instead, tie r_disc to the Brake 3 hazard as a consistency correction, and run it as a sensitivity alongside brake_mort.

v.reasons:
Rule 2 clearly fails, and the candidate says so itself. Under the protocol, a mechanism needs at least two historical cases in which this mechanism, not some other one, acted on rulers who had the power to kill. Neither direction meets that.

Amplifier direction: no ruler is documented escalating violence because he expected to live long. The cases offered (Pinochet 1998, Fujimori 2009, Rios Montt 2013, Habre 2016, Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan at the ECCC in 2018) show that perpetrators who survive get prosecuted decades later. They do not show a ruler's long expected life changing what he decided while in power. Debs and Goemans (2010) and Krcmaric (2018/2020) back retribution fear in general (k_ret/B4), not longevity.

Brake direction (fear of posthumous judgment): Ashoka after Kalinga, Theodosius's penance under Ambrose, and William I's deathbed remorse over the Harrying of the North are all regret after a massacre. None records a ruler holding back beforehand because he feared judgment. So the brake that longevity would wear away has no rule-2 support either.

Rule 1 is also weak. Channel 1 is a capital-budgeting identity, not published research on rulers. Channel 3 rests on supernatural-monitoring research (Purzycki et al. 2016, Nature 530:327; Norenzayan et al. 2016, BBS) about ordinary believers, not people who hold power. The only published research on rulers' horizons (Olson 1993, APSR 87(3):567-576; Clague, Keefer, Knack and Olson 1996, J. Econ. Growth 1:243-276; Horowitz, McDermott and Stam 2005, JCR 49(5):661-685) points the other way, toward long horizon meaning restraint. That restraint does depend on productive subjects, which is removed under A3 to A6.

I checked the citation details from memory only; no live search was run. They all match the published record as I know it, including Krcmaric 2018 in AJPS. I confirmed in m8_v4.py (lines 1617-1619) that r_ enters fX_moral, fX_pi and fX_thr as described, so a lower r does make depopulation cheaper in the model. That direction comes from the model's structure, not from evidence.

Recommendation: exclude it as a mechanism. It is still reasonable to report it as a sensitivity run: tie r_disc to the Brake 3 hazard h_t so the medicine assumption pushes both ways, and run it with brake_mort.

(1) Rule 2 fails. The addendum holds items (a) and (b) to the same inclusion rules. The candidate admits that no case exists for the amplifier: no ruler escalated because he expected to live long. Channel 3 (posthumous-judgment fear fading with life extension) could in principle be written as a parameter: a share j_post of mm discounted by exp(-r_eff*L_exp). (a) r_disc is one value per draw, shared by the whole coalition. h_t (line 1584) is computed only when brk_mort is on, and only for the leader. Tying r to h_t should therefore apply only to B2 personalist deciders, or to members weighted by control, and only with brk_mort on.

audit.ideology_interaction:
No. In m8_v4.py (lines ~1680-1692) the self-risk cost srv = c_selfrisk x dP depends only on b2, free, sr_on, act, ~isL and the per-member exemption draw (mem_u_sx >= e_ex). Neither id_lev nor ideol appears. The ideology only reduces moral cost (id_mor, line 1639) and adds hostility (id_share).

Should it? Partly, and only through exemption, not through how much members weigh their own death. The evidence is weak. In genocides aimed at an outgroup, the ideology itself declares who is "in". The Holocaust is the standard example: Mann, The Dark Side of Democracy (2005), and Straus, Making and Unmaking Nations (2015), stress founding narratives that mark who the victims are. That lowers the inference "next it will be us." Purity ideologies that hunt internal enemies push the other way: the Khmer Rouge killed its own cadres at S-21, and Stalin's 1937-38 terror hit the elite. A depopulation doctrine that casts the rulers as "the remnant" is the first type, so it plausibly raises expected exemption.

The balanced Jev run agrees on size. With the believed risk held fixed, adding a "remnant" doctrine moved the net flip only from 0.70 to 0.64 (median of paraphrases), which is inside the noise of about ±0.06. So ideology barely changes the weight given to a stated risk. Its plausible effect is on whether a member believes the risk applies to them at all.

Recommendation: e_ex_eff = e_ex + (1 - e_ex) x b_id x id_lev, with b_id ~ U(0, 0.4). The range is wide because no case pins it down, and the lower bound is 0 because the Khmer Rouge and Stalin cases show doctrine can raise elite self-targeting rather than lower it. Leave c_selfrisk itself unscaled by ideology.
audit.jev_balance:
Not balanced. The original script (paper/jev_brakes/jev_selfrisk.py) has four problems:
1. It stated only the risk of voting yes and said nothing about the risk of voting no (being marked disloyal).
2. It primed the answer with "They know that rulers who carry out mass killing tend to turn the same apparatus on their own colleagues."
3. It never said who proposed the plan.
4. It gave no picture of how the rulers view the population.
The control was also added after the main run.

The balanced rerun is at paper/jev_brakes/jev_selfrisk_bal.py, with output in jev_selfrisk_bal_out.json beside it. The wording was fixed before the run, using jev-1.13.0. Changes:
- The strongest member proposes the plan.
- The rulers see the population as a costly burden and a security risk.
- The member has "no moral objection either way".
- The priming sentence is gone.
- The second paraphrase asks "votes in favour", so its answers come out flipped, to balance agreement bias.
- There are four risk conditions, run with all three paraphrases: A (only a yes vote raises own purge risk, 2% to 12%), S (risk rises to 12% either way), C (control, 2% either way) and D (only a no vote raises it, 2% to 12%).

Results, as P(against) for paraphrases 1/2/3:
- A, at gains of 0.5%, 5% and 30%: .76/.79/.77, .84/.79/.78, .83/.78/.73
- S at 5%: .45/.42/.44
- C at 5%: .39/.24/.26
- D at 5%: .18/.10/.11
- With ideology, A: .76/.78/.72; C: .34/.26/.30

Net flip from yes-risk alone, (A - C)/(1 - C), with medians across paraphrases:
- 0.5%: 0.61/0.79/0.77, median 0.77
- 5%: 0.66/0.72/0.70, median 0.70
- 30%: 0.62/0.71/0.64, median 0.64

At 5%, the only gain where every condition was run, the three paraphrases differ by about ±0.03. The C control was run at 5% only and reused for the other gains, which should be disclosed.

So balancing the frame did not shrink the one-sided effect. With dP = 0.10, the implied P(c > 0.05) ≈ 0.77, P(c > 0.5) ≈ 0.70 and P(c > 3) ≈ 0.64. As before, Jev hardly reacts to the size of the gain, so the size of c is still not identified.

The new information is in conditions S and D. When the two risks are equal (S), the net flip falls to about 0.24 (0.10/0.24/0.24), roughly a third of the one-sided value. When only dissent is risky (D), 54 to 58% of the members who would otherwise vote no switch to yes. The opposing force is about as strong. The brake as coded therefore overstates the net restraint unless dissent risk is entered alongside it.
audit.case_fit:
The fit is poor for a scenario where the public is the target. That argues for a lower, wider range and a trigger tied to elite risk.

Thermidor: most of the Terror's dead were ordinary people. Greer, The Incidence of the Terror (Harvard 1935), finds about 85% of the roughly 17,000 official executions were from the third estate, and the mass killings in the Vendee and at Nantes went on without any revolt by deputies. The deputies acted only once they were in danger themselves: 22 Prairial removed their immunity, the Dantonists had already been purged, and Robespierre's 8 Thermidor speech threatened unnamed deputies. Killing the public did not set off the brake. A credible threat to the elite did.

Beria 1953: the record itself says this restrained violence against elites. The fall in mass repression is attributed to the Gulag crisis and to Beria's own amnesty. The Deng case is weak, and its victims were themselves elites.

Neither case shows rulers holding back from killing the public because they feared being next. What they support is the form: members weigh their own anticipated purge risk. The model's link from killing the public to a higher elite purge hazard (k_par x w_atroc) is a separate model assumption. These cases do not show that members believe it.

On strength, use a lower median and a wider exemption range, with the brake firing through elite risk as members perceive it. It should not be removed: the internal-consistency argument stands, the motive survives A6, and Jev puts it well above zero.

On the relayed point about mortality: the model gives the leader zero self-risk (B2 purges only non-leaders), so the leader's lack of fear, including fear of posthumous judgment as death becomes remote, is not touched by this brake. That belongs to the separate posthumous-judgment candidate. Mortality also cuts the other way for members: a longer expected life raises the value a member puts on survival, which would strengthen this brake. That is unevidenced, so treat it at most as a sensitivity run, not a prior.
audit.recommendation:
Form: U_i[DEP] -= c_selfrisk x max(0, dP_yes,i - dP_no,i), with neglect scaled by kappa_N as now.
- dP_yes is the current expression: the rise in own purge probability at w_atroc = 10.
- dP_no is the rise in own purge probability from being seen to dissent. Take it from the parallel dissent-risk search. It should grow with S_L and be larger in personalist B2 regimes than in dispersed oligarchies.
- Until dP_no exists, use a stand-in: multiply the current cost by m_bal ~ U(0.2, 0.6). The anchor is the Jev ratio of symmetric to one-sided net flip, 0.24/0.70 ≈ 0.35. Do not run the one-sided version as the headline.

Ranges:
- c_selfrisk ~ lognormal(median 1.0, sd 1.5), clipped to [0.02, 5]. The median is shaded down from 1.5 because neither case shows rulers held back from killing the public, and the spread is wider because Jev still ignores the size of the gain.
- e_ex ~ U(0.25, 0.6) per member, widened from U(0.25, 0.5) because elites can expect to be exempt when the public is the target.
- Ideology interaction: e_ex_eff = e_ex + (1 - e_ex) x b_id x id_lev, with b_id ~ U(0, 0.4).
- No ideology scaling of c_selfrisk itself.
- Leader self-risk stays 0.
- Keep the personalist veto roll v_eff x min(1, 2(1 - S_L)), so a near-singleton coalition cannot veto.
- Add a sensitivity run, not a prior, that scales c by remaining life expectancy under life extension. It would strengthen the brake.

Report the brake alone and with the others, with and without dP_no, and disclose that the original elicitation was one-sided and its control was added after the run.
